Fisher developed the Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection using the concepts of average excess and average effect, where he initially defined the average effect as the product of a specific allele frequency and the standardized effect of a single allele. However, he later changed it to the average effect of all alleles, but still used the standardized effect, which had no clear biological meaning, and was essentially measuring the correlation, not the causation, in genetic terms. This change of variables was not clearly explained and was considered 'a bit horrible' by Hirschleben, who however found an alternative interpretation. This study reveals that Fisher's variables were part of a broader problem involving the optimization of a multivariate function under constraints and shows that a causation measure can be developed using the methods of homology and orthogonal projection. Fisher's original variable has been rediscovered and, along with the method of orthogonal projections, has potential applications in other fields of statistics. This study also highlights the significant role of Fisher's fundamental theorem in the history of evolutionary biology and statistics. Despite its simplicity, this mathematical solution has far-reaching implications for the complex relationship between correlation and causation in genetic studies. This finding is particularly significant in the age of big data and genetic research, where the distinction between correlation and causation is crucial for understanding the mechanisms of natural selection and making inferences about the causes of genetic effects. This distinction is essential for understanding the underlying biological mechanisms and making accurate inferences about the causes of genetic effects, which is critical in the fields of evolutionary biology and statistics. This study proposes a new measure of causation and shows that this measure aligns with Fisher's original variable. Fisher's fundamental theorem has the potential to answer the long-standing question of whether genetic variations are the cause of evolutionary changes or simply a by-product of them. This theorem, when applied to optimization problems in evolutionary biology, can help determine whether genetic changes are responsible for evolutionary changes or simply a by-product of them. This study presents a new method for developing causes of genetic effects, which is critical in understanding the mechanisms of evolutionary changes and making inferences about their causes. Decentralized learning technique, federated learning, has a major limitation that remains to achieve optimal performance due to statistical data discrepancies. Overcoming this issue, a novel approach called Federated Selective Sharing (FSS) is introduced, which enables clients to send trained models based on customized data subsets. FSS addresses the issue of clients with limited labels by implementing a data efficient procedure. Moreover, a performance enhancing technique, called Model Enhanced Selection (MES), is introduced which ensures that only high quality models are shared with updated parameters. Experimental results on Formulaa and ImageNet datasets demonstrate that FSS leads to significant improvements of up to 4% compared to the current best practice, FedBuff, with substantially reduced communication costs. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of communication costs and performance trade-offs is conducted. The code for this research is available on GitHub at the link https://github.com/krish-yo/FedBuff-FSS-MES. Dataset can be obtained from https://github.com/ElementsOfBIOinformatics/tree/main/formulae. This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions. Next, we outline a criterion for monitoring the convergence of a conditioned process to its quasi-stationary equilibrium and, through numerical examples, demonstrate the practical application of this criterion in assessing the conditioned process's limit behavior. Finally, we generate fresh conclusions regarding the upper bounds for the rate of convergence and speed of approach to the quasi-stationary equilibrium. In particular, we derive non-asymptotic error estimates for Monte-Carlo simulations involving Markov chains with finite state spaces. In the course of our analysis, we identify and discuss two notable inequalities - the log-Sobolev inequality and the hypercontractivity inequality - in relation to the rate of convergence of a conditioned process. We establish that a conditioned process possessing a bounded backward probability can be monitored using a criterion based on the total variation distance to its quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate, and that this same criterion may also be applied to evaluate the performance of Monte-Carlo algorithms for sampling from a Markov chain with a finite state space. We show, for instance, that this criterion effectively detects the convergence in a Monte-Carlo simulation of a conditioned Ising model to a quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific conditions. We anticipate that this criterion will prove useful in assessing the convergence of a wide array of conditioned processes, such as those including a conditioned mean-field model of the Curie-Weiss type, a conditioned contact process, a conditioned voter model, a conditioned Moran model, a conditioned selection-mutation model, a conditioned Kimura 2-parameter model, a conditioned coalescent process, a conditioned model one step below the coalescent, and others. To better assess the Emergency Department's admission process, we analyzed average response curves for treatment duration. Extending the time for treatment is considered an effective strategy for improving admissions; nonetheless, empirical evidence supporting this approach is scarce due to the difficulties in discontinuing treatment mid-way. A key challenge lies in identifying equivalent treatment periods that can be terminated or prolonged. In an attempt to address this issue, we developed a novel direction metric tailored specifically to abdominal pain patients, which is grounded in symptom assessment. Our findings show that optimizing admission rates for these patients necessitate either terminating treatment at 220-240 minutes or prolonging it to 260-280 minutes, both of which require discontinuation at the optimal metric. As a result, treatment can be optimized by terminating it at the 220 minute mark and replacing the difference with a nil treatment protocol, yielding an increased admission rate at the end of the treatment duration. Furthermore, we proved the robustness of our model by conducting sensitivity analysis on various pain assessment tools. Ultimately, terminating treatment at 220 minutes was found to enhance admissions without the need for ongoing treatment discussion with patients. Consequently, we propose this approach as a valuable tool for optimizing Emergency Department treatment duration. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options. Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has shown effectiveness when tailored to a single organisation, but combining data from multiple sources is challenging due to data format inconsistencies and privacy concerns. To address this issue, this paper introduces a collaborative federated learning framework, allowing multiple organisations to co-create and train a robust ML-based intrusion detection system without compromising their data's privacy. A key feature of the proposed framework is the ability to collect and process network traffic data in a common format to reveal meaningful patterns. The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-established concern in manufacturing. Solutions have commonly drawn on a variant of the classic Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), with a focus on achieving the quickest or most time-efficient task sequence. Despite their optimality, these methods face challenges in real-time execution, especially with larger problems. In fast-paced online planning environments where tasks are executed swiftly, the time taken to optimize task ordering becomes a substantial hindrance, even overshadowing the overall task duration. The optimal approach in such cases involves balancing solution quality with total task expenditure, achieving a suitable balance between time efficiency and optimality. The proposed algorithm achieves this through an iterative process of sequential task ordering, leveraging a modified memory-efficient TSP variant. It achieves optimal results with minimal memory usage, enabling fast online planning by efficiently allocating computational resources. The approach also accommodates various online planning variations, including routing with obstacles and a task prioritization variant known as Priority TSP. The study evaluates its performance against a range of benchmark datasets and cutting-edge algorithms from the industry, demonstrating significant enhancements in time efficiency and optimality without prioritization, and comparable results with prior best performances when prioritization is in use. The study's findings are also expanded into a Python package, readily accessible through GitHub at the address https://github.com/alexalexalex97/Optimal-Sequential-TSP. The package offers a flexible and easily interpretable solution, enabling its use in a variety of online planning contexts. The package's usage is simple: users need to replace the provided sample tasks with their own, specifying either a 2D or 3D prioritized or non-prioritized task sequence. The package then generates and shows the optimal sequential TSP solution, ready for use in robot planning. The study documents its computational costs, demonstrating fast online applicability with processing times under 10 milliseconds when using the prioritized variant. The study's solutions show promise in a range of practical applications in robotics and aerospace, among others, as exemplified through its application in routing tasks for a warehouse robot. The study successfully utilized the proposed algorithm to achieve optimal task sequences in various numbers of tasks, ranging from 20 to 400. The algorithm showed fast convergence to optimal results, especially with prior research orientations towards efficiency over prioritization. The study demonstrates the potential for online planning by achieving optimal results in fast sequences with roughly double the time of the task count. The capacity of wireless networks is inherently restricted by interference, and there has been a lack of investigation into the correlation of interference, which has the potential to cause substantial delays in local transmission. This study addresses the query of whether randomizing the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer, using protocols like frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA, can mitigate the adverse effects of interference correlation. By deriving precise analytical expressions for the mean and variance of local transmission delays in both protocols, and determining the optimal parameters that minimize these delays, this study proposes two distinct operating modes, correlation-limited and bandwidth-limited. Notably, while both protocols may exhibit identical mean local delays when operating at specific conditions, their variances diverge significantly. Finally, this study evaluates the interplay between delay and variability, and provides crucial bounds on the local delay tail probability, offering valuable insights for wireless system design. To facilitate practical application, this study transforms the constrained Markov chain into a sequence of independent and memoryless Markov chains, which are analyzed to uncover the statistical properties of the local delay. Furthermore, this study examines the effects of interference on the performance of ALOHA, and reveals that, unlike FHMA, ALOHA is incapable of entering a state that is both correlation-limited and bandwidth-limited. Additionally, when operating in the bandwidth-limited mode, this study shows that the local delay of ALOHA can be approximated by the sum of two independent delays: the delay resulting from interference from adjacent transmitters and the delay resulting from interference from distant transmitters. This distinction allows for the derivation of a simplified expression for the local delay of ALOHA, and offers valuable insights into the operating characteristics of this protocol in wireless systems. In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of the interplay between delay and variability in wireless systems, and provides essential bounds on the local delay tail probability, both of which are significant contributions to the field. Moreover, the findings of this study can be applied to multiple systems beyond those examined here, and are expected to have a substantial impact on wireless system design. For instance, future research could center on evaluating the effects of channel fading on wireless system performance, which could provide valuable insights into the operating characteristics of wireless systems. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions to classification. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents local neighborhoods through mutual information maximization. To counterbalance the risks of pseudo-label noise and class imbalance, we also incorporate a modified cross-entropy loss with class-balanced regularization in the model re-training process. Comprehensive experiments on six graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, which outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and robust self-supervised methods on graph-related tasks. The source code for InfoGNN can be found at https://github.com/jaykim9876/InfoGNN.

In video processing tasks, precise identification of recognizable objects at a low computational cost enables real-time video analysis on devices. We present PatchNet, a highly efficient neural network model for tracking objects across adjacent frames in videos. Unlike traditional pixel-based approaches, PatchNet leverages patch-wise correlation features. This results in a compact network that runs at a remarkably low computational cost of 58MFLOPs, approximately $5\times$ simpler than MobileNetV2. Our research showcases the effectiveness of PatchNet on object detection in videos and visual tracking, yielding substantial performance gains and comparable or even better results. Specifically, on benchmark datasets ImageNet VID and OTB2015, PatchNet significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art models by reducing their computational costs, often with little to no decrease in accuracy. Furthermore, experiments on low-power hardware, such as the Jetson Nano, reveal 2.8x to 4.3x speed improvements resulting from the computational savings achieved by PatchNet. We visually illustrate the advantages of patch-wise feature learning over pixel-based learning through a feature mask and a feature map, showing that patch-wise learning identifies recognizable objects at a lower computational cost while capturing essential cross-frame spatial structure information to support object detection in videos. Our research also discusses the design principles and key innovations behind the new approach. In addition, we provide further improvements over the OTB2015 benchmark using ensembles and ensemble distillation to En-Net with successful results on certain tasks. Our work on patch-wise feature learning opens up new avenues for efficient video processing applications. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it's essential to accurately distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which poses a challenge as current methods are incomplete. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. Leveraging a weighted least squares optimization framework, we employ statistical features derived from bivariate histograms and specific image characteristics, which are then used to train a classifier for binary classification of smoke or non-smoke content. We have tested our approach on the Cholec80 dataset and achieved notable results, demonstrating a 4% improvement in accuracy and F1-score over standard RGB image performance, as well as enhanced performance compared to existing methods. Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and have limited lifespan due to
imperfect gate operations. To work effectively with these processors, compilers
must optimize programs to run within the device's coherence time, translating them
into the most efficient version possible to extract maximum value from the hardware.
We have developed new, deterministic methods to efficiently compile repetitive quantum
circuits within a short period of time. Specifically, these patterns are found in
circuits that use the variational quantum eigensolver to study molecular systems and
RyRz heuristic approach to wave function. We've demonstrated that our pattern-based
compilation approach, combined with an efficient program swapping strategy, results in
optimized programs, comparable to the best compilers available today in terms of CNOT
count and depth, while also performing nearly as well as possible in terms of measurement
count. Not only did we improve compiler efficiency, but our methods now allow for the
reuse of compiled programs at different levels of hardware abstraction, further boosting
performance. With the current generation of quantum processors, our compilers offer an
average depth improvement of 1.5 times the original compiler efficiency, and 2 times
the efficiency of the program swap compiler. Moreover, our new compilers are scalable
for large molecular complex simulations and can be easily adapted for other quantum
algorithm implementations. We've made our compilation tools and programs available for
public use at https://mcqst.github.io/compilers/ and https://github.com/McQST/pqrz.

Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats. In this investigation, two strategies for creating the most efficient engines are considered, specifically (1) using hybrid quantum systems capable of performing multiple beneficial tasks, and (2) minimizing random fluctuations in these tasks. In classical devices, eliminating random fluctuations requires high entropy generation as dictated by thermodynamic uncertainty principles. Additionally, we explore the influence of charge conservation restrictions on its performance. Furthermore, our research also identifies a new quantum tool for reducing random fluctuations in heat transmission, presently not replicable but worth noting for future innovation. Lastly, we examine the relationship between strongly nonlocal interactions within the double quantum dot and the exceptionally high cooling rates achieved by our device. In conclusion, our study showcases the exceptional potential of hybrid quantum systems for advanced thermal engineering applications. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model, SQL-CrossLint, over baseline models SQL-CrossNet and Type-Control, with a notable improvement in accuracy. Moreover, our model's absorption capability and domain adaptation ability are verified through the conducted experiments. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. The results also showed that the collective 2+ state had a strength similar to the collective 2+ state in 58Ni, and that the excitation energy of the first 0+ state was 2.1 MeV, with a magnitude of strength 0.17, indicating a significant departure from the energy vs strength trend observed in the Ti and V region. The findings suggest that the 64Ni nucleus has a unique combination of the epsilon and gamma vibrational phonons, and for the first time, the E(e) band was observed in a Ni isotope, with a maximum spin of 10+ and a strength of 3.4. The study's data resolved the 5+ 2+ puzzle by identifying a collective 2+ state at 2838 keV, separated from the 5+ state by 76 keV, and explained its high energy through a collective 2+ interaction. Active galactic nuclei with exceptionally powerful radio signals are among the brightest known celestial sources, spanning across a wide range of wavelengths. These powerful jets from supermassive black holes can significantly influence both the black hole's growth and its surroundings in the vast expanse of space. In the radio spectrum, these jets can be observed on various scales, but their X-ray and gamma-ray emissions are predicted to be concentrated on smaller scales, typically under 10 parsecs. Recent findings by the Chandra X-ray telescope have revealed the presence of kiloparsec-scale jets, which has sparked debate about the source of their high-energy radiation. Understanding the origins of this high-energy radiation is essential for accurately determining the physical properties and powers of these large-scale jets, which in turn affects the environment in which they reside. In this investigation, we explore the potential for the Inverse Compton interaction between relativistic electrons in jets and cosmic microwave background photons as a plausible explanation for the observed high-energy radiation of these large-scale jets. In specific, we examine three renowned objects: 3C 120, 3C 270, and NGC 1265, which have been well-studied with Chandra, to see if the Inverse Compton model offers a viable solution to their X-ray gap problem. The results of our investigation show that this Inverse Compton model is a plausible explanation for the X-ray luminosities of these objects, which are observed at a distance of about 1 kiloparsec. Moreover, our model also provides a practical method for estimating the physical characteristics of relativistic jets over large scales, which are not easily accessible through other observations. The model's prediction for NGC 1265 is that its X-ray emission is likely to decrease as we move towards its lobes, which is supported by the available Chandra observations. Conversely, the model's prediction for 3C 270 is that its X-ray emission is likely to increase as we move towards its lobes, which is also supported by the available Chandra observations. In conclusion, our investigation shows that the Inverse Compton model offers a viable solution to the X-ray gap problem for these large-scale jets and can be employed as a practical method for estimating their physical characteristics over extended scales. The model's validity needs to be further confirmed by simulating the precise morphology of these jets and their interaction with their surroundings in the vicinity of their black holes. In the vision transformer (ViT) architecture, the use of global averaging as a global pooling method has been prevalent. However, it has been contended that this technique has unintended consequences, such as discarding valuable spatial information and hampering model interpretability. Contrary to these contentions, our study reveals that global averaging exhibits robustness to spatial shifts and eye-catching performance enhancements when slightly modified. We show that this effectiveness stems from the model's ability to learn a global context through attention mechanisms, and propose a novel global learning framework that surpasses the current state-of-the-art ViT performance across ImageNet and ImageNet-V2 benchmarks. We also developed a unique human study to investigate the claims surrounding global averaging, and conducted an in-depth analysis of the ViT model's behavior using various visualization techniques. Additionally, our study highlights the unique characteristics and strengths of ViT models compared to other vision models, and explores the potential applications of global learning in the coming years. We made our study available on our website at https://fairvit.github.io.

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach marks TCube as the first exploration of neural methods for time-series narration, according to our current knowledge. In our comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that TCube significantly improves the variety of words in the generated stories, while also maintaining correct grammar, by up to 65%. Furthermore, an expert review within the geology domain reveals that TCube's narratives are 61% more engaging than existing narration methods. TCube's open-source code and supporting materials are publicly available for anyone to reproduce our results and build upon our work. We hope this research paves the way for the development of other neural methods for time-series narration. TCube has the potential to be an extremely useful tool for data scientists and analysts who work with time-series data, as they will no longer be limited to using traditional, mechanized narration methods. Moreover, the ability to describe time-series data through engaging stories can lead to significant insights and a deeper understanding of the data, according to our current knowledge. We believe TCube can find applications in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. In short, TCube offers a groundbreaking, universal solution for time-series narration that goes above and beyond what is currently achievable with traditional methods. TCube's generated stories are 65% more engaging and varied, along with being 60% more coherent, according to our comprehensive evaluations. Moreover, an expert review within the geology domain reveals that TCube's narratives are 61% more engaging than existing narration methods. TCube's open-source code and supporting materials are publicly available for anyone to reproduce our results and build upon our work. We hope this research paves the way for the development of other neural methods for time-series narration.

This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations and increase the difficulty of accurately segmenting Japanese words. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora. Furthermore, this study showcases the effectiveness of pre-trained word embeddings in enhancing Japanese word segmentation, a technique previously verified in Chinese word segmentation. Lastly, this study compares the performance of LSTM and GRU under identical settings to assess their relative strengths. According to the experimental findings, LSTM consistently surpasses GRU in Japanese word segmentation tasks. In summary, this study confirms the suitability of LSTM for complex tasks like Japanese word segmentation, a challenging problem in natural language processing. In addition to its practical applications, this work makes significant theoretical contributions to the field of natural language processing. In particular, this study sheds new light on the underlying mechanisms of LSTM's performance. Consequently, this study advocates for the adoption of contextualized memory-based models as a fundamental paradigm in natural language processing. This study investigates various theoretical models that account for galaxy diversity, specifically comparing a Self-Interacting Dark Matter model with isothermal core to Cold Dark Matter models with/without baryonic feedback. Contrary to standard CDM, SIDM can form isothermal cores, and may have an upper limit for its cross-section that's compatible with the standard CDM framework. However, further research is needed to determine the precise constraints on this cross-section. Unlike CDM, SIDM is not highly sensitive to long-term baryonic feedback processes like stellar/fossil gas consumption, and ultimately forms similar cores in galaxies, regardless of initial density. This process is accelerated by stellar/baryonic feedback in galaxies with high initial density. Despite not requiring feedback to determine core radius, baryonic processes still play a significant role in determining the galaxy's outer profile. This is because feedback determines the ratio of a galaxy's dark matter halo mass to its baryonic mass, and thus influences the final profile. This study uses simulation data from a specific set of galaxy models to determine the impact of varying cross-section values on core formation, and compares these findings to CDM models with/without feedback for reference. A brief summary of baryonic feedback's effects on core formation is provided, and areas for further research are suggested. resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To overcome initial adoption hurdles,
our system employs a vast knowledge base that maps climate causes and effects to relevant personal values.
Given the absence of a complete climate knowledge base, we revisit knowledge acquisition techniques and construct
a database through natural language analysis of publicly available sources. To foster further research and applications,
the knowledge base and its code will be made open-source for the scientific community. 
To evaluate the effectiveness of our system in stimulating climate conversation and inspiring action,
we plan to conduct a pilot study where participants with varying levels of interest and experience in climate issues will be engaged. 
The system's capabilities and potential benefits, along with the pilot study's objectives and requirements, are detailed in this article.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specialties. 
To reduce dependency on specific data, we develop an adaptive strategy for extracting symptoms by temporarily removing commonly mentioned symptoms from the original data source.
Also, our proposed approach pre-trains the language model using relevant but unmarked text for enhanced data representation. 
Experimental results show that incorporating these strategies significantly enhances symptom extraction accuracy when comparing source and target datasets. 
This method's effectiveness is validated through evaluation of accurate symptom event extraction using established evaluation metrics. 
Our research computes symptom event extraction metrics on three publicly accessible datasets named MIMIC-III, Charite, and PhysioBank. 
Finally, we analyze the predictive performance of the adaptive strategy on unseen symptom events by using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve as the performance metric. 
This research's techniques and resources are made available to the public for replication and future use. 
Source code can be accessed via this link https://github.com/Imagimagnin/adaptive_symptom_extraction, while the dataset can be found at https://datadrivetrain.github.io.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology has now enabled the acceleration of neural networks by several orders of magnitude, but the development of a universal algorithm for converting neural network models into spike-based systems has yet to be achieved. Current methods typically compromise on efficiency, complexity, or portability from one platform to another. This research introduces a novel framework for creating spike-based neural networks by converting their weights into manageable spike transmission strengths over feasible numbers of synapses. The study evaluates this framework against rival methods and showcases its applicability on a computer vision task using a Inmercian Pegasus P20-32P neuromorphic processor with 352 neurons and substantial latency reduction for synaptic operations. The results indicate a notable delay in processing time but a marked reduction in computational requirements: a typical model took 1.48 milliseconds to process on the processor, compared to 4.17 milliseconds for a equivalent software-based algorithm on a standard CPU. This processor-based solution outperformed a comparable GPU-based algorithm by a factor of 2.33. The study also demonstrated the effectiveness of this framework with various neural network models and diverse workload types, yielding significant operational cost savings of up to 75% off current deep learning-based architecture implementations. The research concludes with a performance comparison of three rival conversion methods, showcasing their advantages and limitations, and suggesting promising avenues for further research in this field. The developed framework has been made freely available to the public on the GitHub platform. Nonetheless, considerable challenges and unanswered questions remain in the field of converting neural networks into spike-based systems. The study finally presents a set of universal guidelines for designers of neuromorphic computing technology to consider when handling neural network workloads on such platforms. A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize these devices via volunteer computing. To take advantage of this opportunity, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system capable of efficiently parallelizing demanding applications across a vast number of personal devices. Pando's innovative approach lies in utilizing a distributed virtual machine on multiple devices to execute tasks simultaneously, while also minimizing data transfer occurrences, which typically cause delays. Moreover, Pando's user-friendly interface enables easy access to a vast pool of resources, allowing users to run applications on a massive grid of computational power. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we performed a detailed evaluation of Pando, achieving remarkable results by speeding up the execution of demanding applications, such as data analytics and graph processing, by a substantial factor over traditional approaches. Additionally, Pando's benefits extend to providing users with the opportunity to utilize a massive, volunteer-based grid of computational power, comparable to large-scale supercomputers, while also introducing novel fault-tolerant techniques for coping with potential errors. Throughout our study, we thoroughly examined Pando's performance using over 500 personal devices and 30 applications for volunteer computing. The outcomes of our investigation offer a comprehensive insight into the design of a volunteer computing system, along with its construction, implementation, and detailed testing. Based on our research, we conclude that Pando represents a significant advancement in volunteer computing, and its future enhancement and promotion are warranted to further expand the scope of applications that can benefit from parallel processing. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results in various areas, such as Krieger embeddings, survivor sets, Hausdorff dimensions, bifurcation sets, and badly approximable numbers. We show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations possess unique properties, specifically that they are winning in Schmidt games and have the countable intersection property. Furthermore, we explore the existence of a rich structure of subspaces and algebras of sets associated with these transformations, then calculate the Hausdorff dimension of various sets, including those derived from Krieger embeddings, bifurcation sets, and the space of badly approximable numbers. Additionally, we introduce a new notion of distance between numbers and demonstrate its compatibility with existing notions of distance. We also identify a new class of sets associated with this distance, which has a unique scale invariance property. In contrast to other methods of assigning distances to numbers, this distance is shown to be compatible with the Lebesgue measure, making it a valuable tool for set construction and the calculation of dimensions. Upon discovering that a set with a particular scale has a Hausdorff dimension of 1, we realize the necessity of developing a new theory of distance numbers. This distance is distinct from other methods in the literature, which it is shown to be incompatible with, specifically the distances proposed by Moran, Schlicht, and Lorraine. Ultimately, the space of distance numbers proves to be too narrow for the construction of the sets in question with a Hausdorff dimension of 1. Consequently, the development of a new, more versatile distance, known as the conservative distance, is required for the construction of these sets. Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Users are generally unable to discern how individual characteristics, or sets of characteristics, influence these models as their values change. In order to improve this understanding, a method called Disentangled Attribution Curves has been introduced to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models through detailed (multi-dimensional) curves depicting feature importance at different variable values. By using this new tool, it is possible to boost the accuracy of regression models and uncover valuable new insights in datasets such as the prediction of life expectancy based on lifestyle and medical conditions. Furthermore, a method for discovering the most influential curves is introduced by utilizing a clustering algorithm to group features with similar attribution curves and identify the most significant ones by assessing their overall importance. The superiority of Disentangled Attribution Curves in extracting relevant and easily interpretable features is demonstrated through a comparison with other commonly used methods on several datasets. Examples in public health and finance have shown that the applications of Disentangled Attribution Curves can result in the development of new feature reduction methods and provide users with a clear understanding of the impact of changing certain features on predictions. The code for this new tool is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Angela-Kang/Disentangled_Attribution_Curves. The repository includes instructions for using Disentangled Attribution Curves on any user-defined dataset and a collection of coded examples are also available there. The reliability and efficiency of Disentangled Attribution Curves have been verified through unit tests and performance analysis. The implementation details and results including time and space complexity are presented in the appendix. Additionally, a detailed overview of the existing methods for extracting the most relevant features from datasets is provided in the literature review and how Disentangled Attribution Curves improve upon these methods are discussed. The contributions of Disentangled Attribution Curves to the field of feature extraction are highlighted and the potential future extensions to this tool are suggested. The benefits of utilizing tree ensemble models are presented and the place of Disentangled Attribution Curves within the broader machine learning field is discussed. The applications of Disentangled Attribution Curves to the prediction of life expectancy and stock price forecasting are used as case studies to illustrate the impact of this new tool. The advantages of discovering the most influential curves using a clustering algorithm are explained and the effectiveness of utilizing this new feature extraction method in communicating results is discussed. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, specifically introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both training and communication times, while remaining robust against adversarial manipulation. Evaluation confirms that Flatee offers a substantial performance gain compared to existing solutions. The source code for Flatee is publicly accessible on GitHub at the provided link. \href{https://github.com/01Rober/Flatee}{https://github.com/01Rober/Flatee}. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and respond to these calls immediately. Unlike other approaches, Timeloops does not rely on static analysis and can support programs written in any programming language. Furthermore, it does not require any modifications to the program or the system calls it uses. Additionally, system call filtering can be performed both locally and remotely by a different system. Validity of the method is demonstrated through comparison with static analysis-based techniques and evaluation of its performance using a wide range of applications and a large number of system calls. The results show that Timeloops can determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make more accurately than other methods and can support a larger variety of programs. Furthermore, it can achieve system call filtering rates comparable to those achieved by static analysis-based techniques while also providing them with additional benefits. The potential uses of Timeloops include improving the performance of system call filters and enabling the development of new system call filter techniques that do not require program modifications. The method of Timeloops is now available as an open-source tool. \end{abstract}

Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for defining linear classification models within curved, high-dimensional spaces that generalize traditional vector-based classification.
Next, we demonstrate that, regardless of the geometry of the space, linear classification models are capable of accurately predicting any $d+1$ data points.
We've formalized the application of these models in complex product space structures and have introduced new types of classifiers for such environments, providing solid theoretical backing for their effectiveness.
Moreover, our analysis reveals that these classifiers can learn complex relationships within high-dimensional data, but we've established that they can only handle at least $d+1$ data points. To substantiate these claims, we tested our methods on various data sets, including synthesized data, image information, and data from single-cell RNA sequencing experiments, observing an approximately $15\%$ average performance gain when applied to low-dimensional representations of the latter data type compared to traditional Euclidean-based classification approaches. The code used for these evaluations can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/charlieropkins/Linear-Classification-in-Complex-Spaces. As the field of deep learning continues to evolve, our analysis suggests that the application of linear models may remain crucial for the effective representation and classification of data residing in complex, high-dimensional spaces, including those that have not yet been fully explored. Stated another way, linear classification will remain a vital technique for at least as many dimensions as the number of data points. The findings reported here provide key insights into the effectiveness of linear classification within complex, product-based space structures composed of diverse geometric environments. The proposed method offers the first linear classification solution for curved spaces beyond Euclidean, and it achieves this through the application of novel neural network-based techniques. This study focused on determining the general equation for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space with a single unit step size, denoted as $|P_n^{d}|$. Our approach began by establishing a recursive relationship for the count formula: $|P_n^{d+1}| = |P_n^d| + 2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} |P_k^d|$. We then presented two distinct methods to derive an explicit equation for $|P_n^{d}|$, involving the application of generating functions and Faulhaber's formula. Ultimately, our findings were presented in a matrix representation as our primary theorem. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, we create a contextual representation for speech, allowing for a systematic incorporation of mask types and contexts. Expanding upon this foundation, we develop a contextual model for speech synthesis by employing bidirectional LSTM on masked speech features. The context model is then integrated with a text-to-spectra analysis model for a comprehensive system. Evaluation of our method on paragraph-level speech demonstrates significant improvements in MOS scores over a vanilla TTS system, with our context-aware strategy outperforming other contextual methods like speech overlap. Furthermore, we enhance speech quality by introducing a context-free speech model that compensates for common speech defects in synthetic speech. The integrated system, MaskedSpeech, surpasses other state-of-the-art speech synthesis systems without the need for post-processing, producing 47.46% more natural samples in terms of the MOS evaluation. Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically during the protostellar and protoplanetary phases.  Past research on binary systems has shown that in these systems, the majority of the acquired mass is typically added to the less massive star, resulting in mass equalization.  Yet, young stellar groups are frequently composed of more than two stars that are predicted to exist in a hierarchical setup.  Notwithstanding the significant astrophysical relevance of this issue, little research has been devoted to understanding differential mass acquisition in systems consisting of three or more stars.  We carried out a study aimed at determining whether the trends of mass acquisition predicted for binary systems are applicable to more complex systems consisting of three or more stars.  Utilizing three-dimensional Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics simulations, our research team used the code Phantom to simulate the dynamic process of mass acquisition in systems consisting of a small binary and a nearby single star.  We identified several distinct phases in these systems: a initial mass equalization process, a subsequent mass disparity due to uneven accretion, dynamical mass instability that caused the mass acquisition process to shift into a high mass disparity phase, and ultimately, the system's thermal equilibrium.  Yet, in systems consisting of a small binary and a nearby single star, the rate of accretion was found to be inversely related to the binary mass ratio.  We found that in systems consisting of a small binary and a nearby single star with a binary mass ratio of 0.1, the rate of accretion was 1% that of systems consisting of a small binary with a binary mass ratio of 0.5.  Conversely, in systems consisting of a small binary and a nearby single star with a binary mass ratio of 0.5, the rate of accretion was 1% that of systems consisting of a single star.  These findings suggest that in systems consisting of a small binary and a nearby single star, the rate of accretion is controlled by the binary mass ratio. This manuscript examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also establish a mathematical framework for generating metric structures from given spatial patterns, and vice versa, without relying on specific assumptions about the universe's homogeneity and isotropy. This approach challenges the widely-held notion that these assumptions are essential for deriving the universe's FLRW metrics from spatial averages. We present concrete examples of intrinsically flat spacetimes with irregular matter distributions, including models with a positive cosmological constant and multiply-connected geometry. These examples demonstrate the diversity of spacetime behaviors possible within this new theoretical framework. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for the existing cosmological paradigm and the need for a deeper understanding of the universe's underlying structure to inform models of its cosmology. We also outline avenues for further research to investigate the properties of intrinsically flat spacetimes in greater detail. Additionally, we provide supplementary materials, including an appendix with further mathematical developments and a glossary to clarify the terminology and mathematical concepts employed in this manuscript. Furthermore, we make available a collection of open questions and projects that are central to the core of this research and can be pursued by undergraduate and graduate students in mathematical physics. We anticipate that our presentation of these examples, combined with the wealth of new theoretical results, will stimulate both insight and innovation within the field of cosmological structure and the study of spacetime dynamics. We believe that our approach to intrinsically flat spacetimes offers a fresh and significant contribution to our understanding of the universe at large. We make our research and associated code freely available to the public through our website at https://www.nkn.com/mf/, where visitors can find additional information, including a list of participants involved in this research and their respective institutions. We would like to extend our gratitude to the participants, collaborators, and family members for their generous support and encouragement throughout this research project. We reserve the right to correct errors or revise content in future editions of this manuscript as necessary. We intend for this presentation to mark the beginning of an exciting new chapter in the study of cosmological theory and the behavior of intrinsically flat spacetimes. We look forward to seeing the impact of this research on the field of mathematical cosmology and to hearing from readers who share our fascination with the universe and its complex behavior within the cosmological paradigm. The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine this process with properties of the cloud specified within a finite sphere of radius. We use a series of models, ranging from simple to complex, to compute steady-state solutions, from Newtonian infall of radial particles to a general relativistic model with particles possessing angular momentum. We compare and analyze the mass accretion rates derived from our models, which include a kinetic description with hydrodynamic Bondi model. Our work specifically looks into supermassive black holes such as Sgr A* and M87*, offering an explanation for their low radiative emission. We find that particles with angular momentum can result in significantly low accretion rates onto the black hole compared to scenarios with no cloud or with particles following a radially directed trajectory. This result is seen in both general relativistic and Newtonian models. In the case of a kinetic cloud with no radial motion, the accretion rate can be higher by a factor of 100 compared to a Bondi model. Our models also show that the kinetic description of infalling particles with no radial motion is consistent with a Bondi model for $\beta 	imes 10^{-3}$, which could imply that the kinetic effect is relevant for masses $10^{3-5}$ solar masses. This comparison allows us to interpret the kinetic effect as relevant for the masses of Sgr A* and M87* if $\beta$ is of the order $10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we find that for particles with angular momentum, a kinetic description yields a higher mass accretion rate by a factor of 100 compared to a steady-state general relativistic model. We speculate that this kinetic effect could provide a theoretical explanation for the low radiative emission observed from the black holes in the galaxy Sgr A* and M87*. This research is the first to show that the merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a black hole can result in a mass accretion rate much lower than predicted by previous models, which could offer a theoretical explanation for the low radiative emission observed from the black holes in the galaxy Sgr A* and M87*. A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without density-induced bias, thus allowing a more accurate understanding of their distribution.  This study, which utilized data from the VOSA, uses absolute magnitudes to select likely O and B stars (totaling 1,042 candidates) in the Galactic disk's outer regions, and, employing 2D cross-correlation, determines their number density patterns in a $20^2$ degree area around the North Pole.  These data show that while many early-type stars are found in small, high-density regions (like molecular clouds and the Gough's Peak/Shorley's Peak structure), a significant population (with a density of ~10^(-2) pc^-2) is found in a vast, low-density area and lacks association with visible star-forming clouds.  This means that a substantial number of massive stars must be found in low-density environments and, given their lower metal content, it is suggested that these stars originate from diffuse, low-density regions.  This, in turn, implies that these massive stars are found in low-density environments both in our Galaxy's outskirts and in less crowded regions closer to the center.  Furthermore, it has been observed that B stars tend to have a higher spatial spread than O stars and, assuming both populations have similar lifetimes, it is suggested that this is due to shorter-lived O star careers before being ejected from their origins.  This research implies that these massive stars originate from locations extending ~20% higher in density than previously thought and, with a smaller share of these stars found outside dense clusters, it is estimated that only ~25% of these stars originate from these crowded environments. Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also enhances the reliability of word embeddings within the documents. This pioneering method differs from conventional binarization techniques, which solely focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating an adversarial network to produce refined output and a reliability metric for gauging the accuracy of word embeddings. Thorough evaluations on diverse handwritten degraded documents indicate that our proposed approach surpasses traditional methods in restoring both visual quality and word embedding reliability. Moreover, by integrating a confidence scaling factor, we demonstrate that our method can be applied to enhance the reliability of word embeddings in real-world, degraded documents. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. In contrast, the larger critical temperature in Nd3RuO7 allowed for a larger ordering effect from the magnetic fields, ultimately resulting in a completely ordered state. Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the symbolic computation of key physical characteristics, such as spin-orbit coupling features and time-reversal symmetry properties. This process took advantage of extensive, pre-calculated data on group cohomology from the GAP4ALPS library. This library is an Arnold-Lapweltshausen collection of algorithms and programs, with calculations performed using the GAP computer algebra system. This project expanded the library by developing new algorithms to compute coset tables and series of subgroups, as well as characteristic polynomials for the non-Gray sets. The resulting data were then applied to determine relevant physical characteristics using a computational framework. The outcomes of these calculations were then compared with theoretical predictions based on topological considerations. The majority of the layer groups showed agreement with these expectations, but some multi-band systems displayed complications that required a more in-depth analysis of their band structures. This study set the stage for further investigations into the symmetry-protected topological properties of these systems, particularly those with gray single groups, by outlining a method to compute topological invariants through a process involving folding and projecting to a torus's surface. Despite these constraints, we were able to calculate the relevant properties for all 80 sets of layer groups and successfully applied a workaround for the computed characteristic polynomials of the high-index subgroups. However, a full resolution of these technical issues is still needed. Lastly, the absence of gray double groups in the compiled data meant that their properties had to be computed numerically, whereas theoretical predictions showed agreement with these outcomes. This study on layer groups contributed to the advancement of topological materials research by addressing an unresolved question in the field. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our study demonstrates the versatility of this approach by applying it to two distinct interacting lattice systems, ultimately gaining up to 100x computational advantage while reaching new theoretical accessibility. Moreover, we successfully extract critical physical information from these simulations, including the equation of state and compression properties of the Hubbard and t-J models. These breakthrough results open doors for similar applications of this method in tackling critical sign problems in lattice simulations. Moreover, the basic architecture of this method can be adapted for solving other differential equations plagued by a sign problem, providing a promising direction for future research. This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous kernel-based ICA methods. In contrast, the proposed m-ar-K-FastICA method offers dynamic kernel adaptation capabilities. Experimental evaluations using built-in datasets and the MNIST dataset for image classification, along with the open-access 'DoppleBaby' dataset for visual domain adaptation, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in comparing independent components, performing robust feature extraction, and achieving improved classification performance. This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic system can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs in a specific category, then a related proof system can do so as well, at roughly the same computational cost. This allows researchers to apply existing bounds from the latter system to the former, shedding new light on CPT's limitations. Establishing a polynomial CPT lower bound via a related PTIME-instance could resolve a long-standing question in finite model theory. Additionally, the findings provide a theoretical explanation for the separation between polynomial calculus and extended polynomial calculus within bounded-degree settings. The paper introduces a new probabilistic version of polynomial calculus, which matches the performance of earlier logic systems in similar contexts. Nonetheless, it's shown that a logic system requiring only a limited number of steps can distinguish non-isomorphic graphs more efficiently than a corresponding probabilistic version of polynomial calculus. The research also explores Tseitin translations, transforming polynomial CPT lower bounds into polynomial CFP (cut-free propositional calculus) lower bounds and revealing a new separation result for bounded-degree polynomial calculus and extended polynomial calculus. The study culminates in a theoretical overview of the connections between FP-catalogs, polynomial logic systems, and extended polynomial calculus. The results provide a new direction for approaching the polynomial CPT lower bound hypothesis via a related PTIME-instance and its potential extension to the general polynomial CPT case. By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Through a novel approach using viapolygons, we achieved the first certification of BNNs with limited data under random data perturbations. The resulting certified solutions outperformed the current state-of-the-art methods on common datasets for robust training, while also exhibiting greater reliability in uncertain predictions and a substantial gain in accuracy under adversarial attacks. Furthermore, our framework is adaptable and can be applied to various certification methods as well as different training techniques. The code for this framework is available on GitHub at https://github.com/gmnwz/certified-bnn.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new transmissions. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for the rate of information dissemination, we reduced this complex phenomenon into a statistical model. Subsequently, we isolated two distinct factors influencing this phenomenon: the propagation speed of the rumor and the rapid growth of its zero-phase. By applying nonparametric and parametric analyses, we found that the latter factor's contribution surpassed the former in areas heavily influenced by news media. Consequently, we developed a metric to gauge a rumor's spread by assessing the proportion of areas where it has penetrated, as calculated through geographic distance analysis, thereby quantifying its severity. Subsequently, we identified critical factors that drive this metric's increase and offer the following practical predictions to mitigate the spread of online rumors in the future: (i) establish early detection mechanisms to detect rumors as soon as possible; (ii) build an accurate database of public health information to substitute unreliable news; (iii) promote digital literacy among internet users to make them less susceptible to consuming unverified information; (iv) implement technologies that can filter and block the propagation of non-verified information. Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework. At the operational level, this harmony condition is seen as an expression of sound reasoning through harmonic configuration, and is further accompanied by an axiom stating that harmonic configurations are always in a state of harmony. This new harmony axiom allows for an independent proof of soundness within the Computational Ludics framework. Finally, this paper undertakes a harmonic reevaluation of the proof of harmony in the intuitionistic natural deduction system, yielding a harmonic proof of harmony, and in the process reveals an alternative, harmonic, version of Prawitz's proof. This approach of deriving proof and harmony separately is seen as embodying a fundamental idea in the Computational Ludics framework. Furthermore, this paper notes that harmonic derivations serve as a means to achieve a soundness result for the cut-free intuitionistic natural deduction system without relying on the cut rule. This result is seen as an independent verification of the traditional cut elimination method used in intuitionistic natural deduction. Finally, this paper offers a harmonic explanation for a renowned result by Prawitz, proving that any harmonic configuration is equivalent to a derivation in intuitionistic natural deduction, and in the process provides an alternative, harmonic, proof of Prawitz's result. This result is seen as an independent verification of Prawitz's original proof. This paper may be seen as an alternative presentation of the contents presented in the PhD thesis of the author. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Our approach also enables users to learn comparative preferences more efficiently by identifying the most significant areas of difference in the state space that have the greatest impact on task-related outcomes. To achieve this, we employ an algorithm that accurately predicts region preferences based on historical comparison data and uses these predictions to guide the labeling process towards the most informative areas, thereby effectively amplifying the human labeling effort. Our experimental findings demonstrate that this combined method yields a substantial increase of up to 43 times better performance compared to individual comparative evaluations, when human labeling time remains consistent. The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome to incorporate potential confounders, then applying predictions to ATE estimators, such as the Average Treatment Effect Williams (AIPW) estimator. In the case of non-parmetric ATE estimators, such as the nAIPW, a Wilcoxon score function is used instead. Both AIPW and nAIPW estimators are based on the Fundamental Theorem of Causal Inference, maintaining parametric model orthogonality and being robust to model mispecification. Although the nAIPW is less susceptible to model pitfalls due to its reliance on a Wilcoxon score function, it faces issues in its application due to the non-existence of its influence matrix. As a result, conventional methods for assessing the variability of ATE estimators, like the delta method, are not applicable. This paper presents an alternative method for evaluating the variability of nAIPW estimators by combining a Wilcoxon score function with a Generalized Linear Mixed Model. This approach enables researchers to leverage established software for mixed models, such as R's lmer, to estimate the variability of nAIPW estimators more efficiently. In order to establish the variance estimator's asymptotic validity, both the Average Treatment Effect Williams and the non-parametric variant are evaluated in simulated experiments before being applied to real-world data from studies on the impact of smoking on lifespan. The results show a strong match between the proposed variance estimator and the variance estimated through bootstrap resampling. This reveals the potential for the proposed nAIPW variance estimator to be a reliable alternative to the traditional delta method. In particular, its efficiency could be seen in its approximately 1.5 times greater accuracy in estimating the standard error of ATE from the smoking studies. This could imply that similar gains in efficiency might occur when applying the proposed nAIPW variance estimator in other contexts. In addition to its potential for improving the assessment of treatment effects, this paper's methodology also offers a newly developed tool for evaluating the performance of causal estimators. This tool enables researchers to assess multiple aspects of estimators, such as bias, variance, mean bias, and bias variance trade-offs - all within a unified framework. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. Finally, parameter values are then easily extracted through a straightforward transformation. Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how complex this transformation can be. Notably, this outcome contradicts traditional transducer equivalences, which were shown to be indeterminable in certain scenarios. This discovery aligns with earlier findings (2018) indicating the impossibility of transforming non-deterministic two-way word transducers into equivalent deterministic models. We also explore similar questions in relation to counter-based transducers and provide a decidability result for an alternative semantics, as well as a further investigation into the fragmented nature of transducer equivalences and their relationships. These results expand our understanding of the complex relationship between two-way and one-way transducer models. We introduce a new notion of 'origin semantics' that diverges from traditional 'classical' semantics, featuring multiple equivalence relations and associated decidability results for various classical and origin semantics on word and counter-based transducers. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between two-way and one-way transducers, showing that origin and classical semantics yield comparable results, whereas classical semantics fails to provide a way to transform non-deterministic two-way transducers into equivalent one-way models, but does so in the case of word transducers. Additionally, we outline a list of open questions and potential future research paths. This study is a culmination of an LPAR conference event, featuring updated and revised presentations.
