However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of zero-shot prompts designed for natural language inference and made them available to the public. Our prompt corpus, dubbed CoSi, comprises 693 instances from 198 distinct prompts, comprising 98 commonly used phrases with variations in sentence structure and the inclusion of answer options. Our analysis of the prompt corpus and the within-prompt factors yields valuable insights that can enhance the creation of tailored prompts and improve the adaptability of large language models. Moreover, by utilizing the CoSi prompt corpus, we demonstrate the creation of customized sets tailored to specific requirements and validate the identification of prompt characteristics that significantly affect the zero-shot performance of state-of-the-art language models when adjusted. Additionally, we contribute the first systematic evaluation of the inclusion of answer choices within prompts – a design element that has been previously overlooked. Interestingly, our results indicate that the inclusion of answer choices is found to have a positive impact on the zero-shot performance of these language models. In line with these findings, the CoSi prompt corpus may serve as a reliable benchmark for researchers seeking to create more practical and user-friendly zero-shot prompts. Moreover, the corpus can inspire innovations in prompt design and provide valuable training data for the development of adaptable language models capable of navigating diverse types of zero-shot prompts. As such, the corpus is poised to contribute to the advancement of both the zero-shot and adaptation paradigms in natural language inference within the broader language model community. The CoSi prompt corpus is available online at https://github.com/yoyoking/CoSi for public use. The repository includes the prompt standardization code and the dataset in the format of an HDF5 file. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical Artin motives, which aligns with Deligne's framework. The construction proposed by Benois hinges on the selection of a regular submodule. When the representation is $p$-regular, choosing such a submodule is analogous to selecting a'motivic' $p$-refinement, making the process fairly intuitive. However, when the representation is $p$-irregular, the process becomes more intricate as it relates to the decomposition of the adjoint representation. Specifically, our work is set within the context of GL$_2(\mathbb{Q})$. The computations of Benois invariants are also accompanied by non-critical instances of the Gauss--Manin conjecture, which describes the relationship between the logarithm of the algebraic part of a certain diagonalizing automorphism and the second logarithm of the algebraic part of the pth-power map. The pth-power map in question is that additive action on the algebraic part of the space of weight one cuspforms that is classical in the critical case. The new cases we consider include weight one cuspforms with irregular adjoint representations and those with a'small' weight one cuspform but an irregular adjoint representation. Our study also identifies a list of cases where the Benois invariants are zero. The time required to compute these Benois invariants is substantially reduced when the representation is $p$-regular. Nonetheless, the computational speed is still impressively high in cases where the representation is $p$-regular. As a result, our work has made accessible a wide range of previously uncomputable instances of the Gross--Benois $p$-adic regulator. Lastly, the algorithm used in this computation is essentially the same protocol used in the calculation of $\mathscr{L}$-invariants by Sasaki. The method is also compatible with unramified regular weights, meaning that under this condition, the Benois invariants are essentially the same as the $\mathscr{L}$-invariants proposed by Benois, which in turn is a refinement of the $p$-adic regulator proposed by Gross. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions occur when high-energy ions surpass the range of the strong force, enabled by virtual photons exchanged between the nuclei, whose numbers directly correlate with nuclear electric charge. Given its exceptional energy levels, the LHC serves as the most powerful photon source ever constructed, particularly in favouring photoproduction of heavy vector mesons due to their inherent affinity to photons. Recent experiments examining the forward J/psi production in lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions at 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector are featured. This study indicates that nuclear modifications affecting the medium are predominantly governed by the nucleus-nucleus collision energy. Furthermore, calculations based on the model of saturation and QCD picture of gluon exchange, taking into account the Landshoff mechanism, show satisfactory agreement with experimental observations when applying a suppression factor to the theoretical results. This outcome is similar to that seen in proton-proton collisions and suggests that photoproduction contributions play a significant role in nuclear collisions. Consequently, the data appear to contradict a scenario in which rapidity density increments stem from gluon nuclear interactions. Model predictions suggesting a modest rise in the rapidity density of prompt J/psi in nuclear collisions, relative to proton-proton collisions, as the collision energy increases from the LHC to the proposed Future Hadron Collider, are also presented. This analysis involves scaling the nuclear modification factor using the scale factor for charmonia and applying momentum and mass constraints in the calculation of the rapidity density of prompt J/psi. This study suggests that photoproduction predictions are a significant component of prompt J/psi production across various collision energies from the LHC to the Future Hadron Collider. The development of modern machine learning algorithms is lagging behind formal requirements. A key concept, essential for ensuring the reliability of models, is the ability to calculate the contribution of each training example to the model's output. This requirement has been overlooked in previous studies, with the exception of those involving linear models that can compute contributions efficiently. However, when dealing with more complex models that utilize neural networks, this computation becomes an computationally intensive task requiring significant time and resources.

A novel method, named LightMINE, is introduced to efficiently perform this calculation on a single GPU, even for large datasets. This method is based on two main components: a layer-by-layer backpropagation framework and a specialized sampling approach called importance awareness. LightMINE is capable of performing this calculation faster than alternative methods while achieving a time complexity of O(n^2.5), exponentially reducing the computational time for large values of n, as demonstrated by extensive testing. Moreover, LightMINE demonstrates high accuracy in contribution assessment, with the ability to integrate this calculation within the model training process using the gradient-based method, revealing previously unknown relationships between examples and their predicted outputs. LightMINE successfully evaluated on 12 image classification tasks, achieving contributions assessments compatible with expert evaluations and meeting the requirements of formal verification. Moreover, LightMINE demonstrates a high level of generalizability, extending its applications to 15 new tasks with minimal modifications and successfully applied to trustworthy model training, data weighting, and example labeling. LightMINE's efficiency in performing these computations without compromising accuracy was achieved through its integration with the specialize-a-little method, allowing it to perform this calculation up to 100 times faster than alternative methods on the GTSB dataset. This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent study of Mn$_3$Sn's transport properties reveals that the effect's disappearance can be attributed to the appearance of a helical magnetic ground state and is supported by in-depth magnetometry and other analyses. Additionally, we discovered that pressure has a significant impact on the material's Hall and Nernst coefficients, as well as the intrinsic spin dilaton, while having only a minor effect on the intrinsic spin relaxation time. Specifically, with each 10% pressure increase, the intrinsic spin relaxation time lengths up by 25%. Our findings not only shed light on the pressure-dependent properties of the anomalous Hall effect but also open up new avenues of research into spin-related phenomena in geometric phases within magnetic materials. The present study serves as a testament to the interconnectedness of pressure-driven transformations in solid-state physics and the potential for the development of innovative and pressure-adjustable technologies inspired by gigapascal conditions. Moreover, it highlights the significance of integrating in situ XRD, SQUID, and other magnetic measurements with transport property assessments to achieve a more comprehensive comprehension of magnetic materials. The pressure-driven properties of Mn$_3$Sn as described in the present study offer a promising foundation for the exploration of similar effects in related materials and can potentially pave the way for the creation of innovative and adjustable technologies inspired by gigapascal conditions. Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to the
domain of formal knowledge acquisition. Although significant advancements have been
made in recent years, the challenging task of relation extraction remains an active
area of ongoing research in the NLP community. This paper aims to provide in-depth
insights into relation extraction, covering key aspects including datasets, models,
datasets, and future prospects for further improvement in the field. A thorough review
of the literature on relation extraction is presented, along with an analysis of the
current state of research in this area and a look towards its future direction. To this
end, the paper seeks to serve as a useful resource for both established and novice
researchers working in the field of relation extraction. One of the key areas explored
in the paper is the potential of applying pre-trained models to relation extraction and
the role of transfer learning in enhancing its performance. Moreover, the paper delves into
the distinct approaches used to extract multiple relations and the different methods for
improving model generalizability on unknown relations. Additionally, the paper covers
the growing applications of relation extraction in the healthcare sector, one of the key
domains where it is being heavily utilized for computing semantic relationships between
medical entities. Overall, the paper seeks to provide an exhaustive understanding of the
state-of-the-art techniques in relation extraction and the knowledge acquisition domain.

Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary. We then discuss how this invariance influences the behavior of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions. Additionally, we derive an approximate expression for the eigenvalue in this scenario when the Robin parameter is set to 0. To support our findings, we showcase several examples that demonstrate the previous claim. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download. Furthermore, we introduce a new benchmark consisting of five small to medium-scale hypergraph datasets that can be used to evaluate the performance of proposed methods. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time open-source hypergraph datasets have been created for the task of supervised hypergraph reconstruction. With this approach, we are able to achieve high accuracy on small-scale datasets, and our best results on a large-scale social network dataset reach an impressive 58.24\% of optimal hyperedge coverage. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time this metric has been used to evaluate this problem. These findings contribute to the advancement of the field by providing significant insights into the effectiveness of proposed methods, as well as the challenges that need to be addressed in future research on supervised hypergraph reconstruction. To facilitate future research, we pose several key questions that need to be addressed in the domain. Additionally, we expand the definition of the structural embeddedness index to hypergraphs, providing a groundbreaking new metric that evaluates the structural completeness of hypergraphs. This innovation marks a significant advancement in the understanding of hypergraph systems, and our analysis of this metric sheds light on its relationships with existing graph embeddings and presents examples of its application in hypergraphs. To conclude, we propose several future research directions that could further refine the structural complete graph model and explore its potential in modeling hypergraphs. These future studies have the potential to contribute substantially to the domain of hypergraph reconstruction. We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a new statistical model for coupled polar and azimuthal degrees of freedom in the emission phase space. This model enables us to derive a cumulative entropy equation for the emission's overall directionality. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that higher gain leads to increased unidirectionality, which aligns with experimental findings. Additionally, we show that our entropy model can distinguish between legitimate single-mode emission and pseudo-single-mode emission caused by mode filtering. Lastly, we apply the emission entropy to analyze the emission pattern of a microcavity laser as it transitions into an unstable robust single-mode emission state. This achievement empowers advanced physics insights into the emission's directional stability and the role of fluctuations in robust single-mode emission. Moreover, it facilitates future applications of entropy in analyzing complex light behaviors in microcavity lasers and other advanced photonics systems. Upon completion of this work, we discovered a previously overlooked connection between the statistical emission model and the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, which presents an interesting case for future research in quantum optics and statistical physics. The one-dimensional statistical model presented in this work can be generalized into a more comprehensive approach to analyzing multi-dimensional phase space emissions. Nonetheless, this straightforward generalization comes with challenges in deriving a cumulative entropy equation, which necessitates further research for its practical application in real-world photonics. Conversely, the new concept of entropy-based unidirectionality provides a measurable quantity for evaluating emission directionality, which can be utilized even in complex multi-dimensional emissions by reducing the dimensionality to the core degrees of freedom. This dimensionality reduction enables the calculation of emission entropy with relative ease, which makes it an attractive option for analyzing complex emission behaviors in modern photonics. In conclusion, the proposed entropy model offers a versatile tool for analyzing the directional emission in a wide range of complex photonics systems. Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model when considering stable relationships with comparators' daily returns, thereby not refuting the efficient market hypothesis. Our research was made feasible by the creation of a customized software, time-series-profiler, which enables rapid and efficient calculation of daily returns and other relevant metrics in large datasets. Additionally, the software's profile functionality enables the visualization of chronological developments in time-series data. The software is now available online at cryclo.com under an open-source license. The evidence presented in this study should contribute to a shift in perception regarding the volatility of cryptocurrencies. Moreover, the approach employed in this research, which integrates financial theory with data-driven statistical analysis, represents a viable methodology for other investigations of economic phenomena. Lastly, the development of the time-series-profiler software offers a useful tool for other researchers. To facilitate reproducibility, all data used in this study are accessible at cryclo.com along with the implementation details of the approach and the software profiled in this research. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. A nonconvex surrogate function and an alternative direction method of multipliers (ADMM) are utilized to improve the low-rank decomposition model's efficiency and computation speed. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques and successfully detects fabric defects. Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework has the potential to increase engagement of fact-based counter-narratives by COVID-19 vaccine skeptics. This framework's first component is based on a long short-term memory unit, which identifies skeptical posts; the second component utilizes a deep neural network to locate relevant counter-narrative content; and the third component, an enhanced graph-based method, increases engagement of the found counter-narratives with skeptical users by incorporating various network metrics. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in increasing counter-narrative engagement of skeptical users through counter-messaging. This framework has the potential to support various social media campaigns by COVID-19 vaccine developers and administrators. Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, in the form of cylinders, were created using a combination of saltwater and heat, and then fired at various temperatures to analyze their internal structure, strength and contraction. The internal structures of these materials were studied under a microscope and their mechanical properties were tested using a universal testing machine. The experiment was performed twice using different types of simulants for Martian and Lunar soil, resulting in manufactured samples resembling traditional building blocks and the initial stages of 3D printing with a binder. The results indicated that the optimal firing temperature for both types of simulants lies between 1100 C and 1200 C. The compressive strength of these materials met the requirements for building structures on other planets, suggesting their potential for use as building materials in extraterrestrial construction and as a base material for additive manufacturing processes similar to 3D printing with a binder. The study also indicated that the materials' strength and contraction behavior vary depending on their composition and the water content used to create them. The test specimens exhibited a 50-60% decrease in volume and a compressive strength of up to 5.9 MPa, strong enough to support building structures on other planets, at least according to current technology standards. The research has significant implications for using in-situ material processing and additive manufacturing in future human missions to the Moon and Mars. This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from 15 possible characters written by multiple individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, a data-driven and rule-based information extraction technique is applied to break down the labeled data. Following this process, two machine learning models are developed - the first is a binary classifier leveraging a hybrid neural network to discriminate writing inputs from non-writing inputs at an earlier stage, and the second is a hybrid neural network for identifying specific writing inputs. However, due to the constraint of 1024 parameters, the hybrid model's complex architecture must comprise only two layers with parameter limits, ultimately hindering its performance. To overcome this issue, the Ensempler, a model combination technique that uses a parameter-efficient hybrid neural network with two layer architectures, is developed. Despite the limitation, the proposed solution achieves a 55% accuracy level on the validation set with model combination, surpassing the baseline performance. Furthermore, the research introduces S.O.S, an automatic mathematical formula generator that demonstrates novelty and usefulness in the current literature. The key innovation of S.O.S lies in its ability to adapt to the timing of the input data and switch between different states, providing an advantage over existing methods as the challenge demonstrates. However, the solution faces obstacles in the form of 1) the difficulty in balancing the size of the dataset, 2) the challenge posed by the diversity of the handwritten input data, and 3) the complexity involved in identifying sequence information in the mathematical expressions. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on the phone sequence domain. We explore a median-based synthesis strategy within this framework, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling synthesis at arbitrary points in time. Experimental results indicate that this method performs comparably to state-of-the-art approaches in predicting the median duration of phone sequences. Additionally, a combination of early and late decisions for phone transition modeling yields superior accuracy in phone transition medians and outperforms current methods for speech segmentation tasks. This new approach possesses the ability to extend its capabilities beyond speech processing and can be applied to modelling sequences in other domains. To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a variational autoencoder trained on extensive, mock spectral series derived from the explosion and evolution models of  Zelig supernovae. The difference between observed and model-based spectral time series proxies is addressed through a kernel-based operator that regularizes the variational autoencoder. The pipeline is validated on realistic data and extensive Monte Carlo simulations, and the results indicate that the variational autoencoder effectively captures the intrinsic trend of SN-Ia spectral evolution, while the kernel-based operator ensures that the model remains robust against the noise inherent in real observations. The research highlights the potential of combining explosion and evolution models with machine learning methods to improve the classification and characterization of SN-Ia supernovae. We further demonstrate that the model can effectively classify normal and interacting SN-Ia supernovae, and that its probabilistic output variances effectively identify uncertainties. The research ultimately suggests the utility of this pipeline for analyzing real SN-Ia data once more extensive mock observations and explosion/evolution models become available. The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access task using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset and demonstrated improved performance compared to systems utilizing standard, non-adaptive activation functions. Notably, we found that the speech synthesis scenario performed more reliably than the voice alteration scenario, with our proposed system resulting in a 6.9% elevation in equal error rate (EER) compared to the voice alteration versus natural speech case, while achieving a 4.6% reduction in EER within the speech synthesis versus voice alteration case. This improvement in performance is a significant advancement towards enhancing the identification of spoken spoofing. We anticipate that the incorporation of AReLU into our system will provide comparable benefits in future applications. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This technique offers a promising approach for in situ characterization of local loss mechanisms in quantum circuits, ultimately enabling the development of better devices. We believe that near-field terahertz investigations have the potential to play a significant role in the advancement of quantum technology. This methodology is adaptable to a broad spectrum of materials and can be employed to study various types of substrates and devices. Moreover, this research is affiliated with the 'Nanofocus' program at Chalmers Microscopy and Materials Research, emphasizing its pivotal role in advancing the field.

Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed inspection. Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, solely relying on static characteristics like port numbers proves inadequate in today's dynamic network environments. As a result, advanced and adaptive approaches are introduced to enhance protocol detection, involving machine learning, feature selection, and hybrid analysis methods. This research investigates the efficacy of these techniques, presenting an innovative method called HyDPC, which uses a complex data representation to integrate deep packet features, network traffic patterns, and volume to enhance application protocol detection. By adopting a feature selection technique within a machine learning framework, HyDPC fine-tunes its prediction model to achieve improved accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that HyDPC surpasses existing solutions in efficiency and accuracy, setting a new benchmark for accurate application protocol identification. Furthermore, the source code is freely accessible on GitHub for further development and utilization. Our study demonstrates the advantages of HyDPC in enhancing the performance of the Yara rule-based NSM framework and other related systems, thereby reducing false positives and streamlining manual review. By integrating with an automatic exploitation tool, HyDPC's predicted protocols are used to trigger customized Yara rule sets, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of the associated exploitation tool. Furthermore, the integration of HyDPC's deep packet features with an existing IP spoofing tool reveals promising outcomes, suggesting the potential for enhanced detection capabilities. The evaluation of HyDPC's scalability and performance across diverse network traffic reveals its ability to efficiently process both large and typical network traffic without compromising its accuracy. Overall, the integration of HyDPC into the nsm-benchmark suite offers a valuable resource for reproducing and validating application protocol identification, thereby supporting the advancement of network security monitoring and related exploitation tools. The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned. To verify the reliability of our results, we conducted multiple experiments and used sophisticated statistical methods to analyze the data. Ultimately, we believe that the breakthroughs achieved by our AI system have the potential to be used as synthetic partners in educational settings to help children overcome counting difficulties. Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively. Additionally, we introduce a new decomposition of divisors that we term the Hodge-Minkowski decomposition, which corresponds to the decomposition of a projective variety into convex subvarieties as described by Belkholdas's theorem. Furthermore, we introduce a new measure to quantify the complexity of a projective variety based on its sectional genus, which we term the genus degree of the variety. This measure allows us to establish a new inequality, thereby extending the accessibility genus degree inequality to all projective varieties, which was previously only established for varieties with the small degree property. Finally, we introduce a new concept of extremal projection, which generalizes the idea of projecting a subvariety from a larger projective variety. This allows us to apply our results to a broad range of geometric situations, including the comparison of projective varieties with differing transcendence degrees, the study of varieties with specified hyperbolic properties, and the investigation of varieties possessing special moduli theoretic properties. Throughout the paper, we seek to clarify the distinct relationships between convex geometry and algebraic geometry, as well as the varied origins and implications of the concepts explored. Our goal is to facilitate the understanding of these interconnected concepts by algebraic geometers familiar with convex geometry. Additionally, we include an introductory section providing a self-contained introduction to the essential principles of convex geometry, as well as extensive references to prior research in the field. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. To facilitate trend analysis, both historical and forecasted price data are considered, with past prices represented by lagging values and forecasted prices represented by advancing values. As a result, the convergence equations appear as finite difference schemes that solve for the maximum trading volume and may differ for efficient and non-efficient market conditions. For efficient markets, a novel nonlinear dynamic system is proposed, along with its corresponding stationary distribution that describes how prices behave over time. To illustrate the effectiveness of this novel approach, both theoretical and practical analyses are conducted, with the latter involving a study of S&P stock market data. Specifically, this application validates the ability of this new method to 1) detect market states, 2) predict price convergence, 3) compare convergence rates for different market conditions, and 4) estimate optimal trading strategies based on real market data. Overall, the proposed approach offers a novel statistical mechanics perspective on market analysis, thereby expanding the scope of applicable market states and providing a more accurate picture of market behavior. Furthermore, the proposed dynamic system and stationary distribution represent a significant breakthrough in understanding market dynamics and may pave the way for future research in this domain. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and precludes data exposure from the server. Notably, it achieves this without incurring substantial computational and communication costs compared to existing learning methods. Finally, FLVoogd's design is collaterally beneficial in that it also prevents data poisoning attacks. FLVoogd's code is publicly available on GitHub at the specified link. Evaluation was conducted on a 40-core Dell server with 512GB RAM and NVIDIA V100 GPUs. Our method supports up to seven users with high memory usage, and we observe a slight performance decrease due to the integration of distance-controlling testing. Nonetheless, it still achieves a training speed of around 3.5 seconds per user. Our method allows the server to make accurate classifications using the central standard model and, upon receiving inputs from three users, to achieve a true positive rate of 0.95 for detecting Byzantine attacks with only a 2% accuracy loss. Moreover, it accomplishes this while maintaining user privacy and incurring only a 10% communication overhead compared to standard FL. Our method's performance gain in communication costs comes from pruning server updates to be 2.5 times shorter, which, in turn, results from applying the same distance-controlling testing to the model updates. Our method's evaluation also demonstrates that the gain in communication costs is coupled with a loss in classification accuracy of around 4%, although this loss could be mitigated by not utilizing distance-controlling testing for model updates. Our method's gain in communication costs is comparable to the efficiency of other systems such as PreSPEAK, which also achieves a 10% communication overhead with a 4% classification loss, but does so through different means. Our method's performance in blocking malicious inputs and precluding data exposure without incurring substantial computational and communication costs highlights its suitability for large-scale deployment. The objective was to create an autonomous vehicle model that navigates a simulated track, adapts to real-world settings, and completes a lap at maximum speed while staying on course. The competition was part of The AI Driving Olympics (AI-DO), a series that fosters embodied intelligence advancements in autonomous driving, by benchmarking the progress in applied autonomy. The Deepracer challenge proved to be complex, especially when translating skills from simulated to real-world settings, so we implemented an innovative approach to transfer learning with a shared neural model. The training of the reinforcement learning agent was done using a modular design, and the results showed a significant margin in performance over run-time optimization and robustness when compared to other submitted entries. Furthermore, our approach allowed for the transfer of skills from the simulated environment to the real-world setting with a speed-up of 100 times in comparison to a model that did not incorporate transfer learning. Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter examines the advancements and difficulties in the production and identification of deepfakes, and also explores the potential solutions to improve the resilience of deepfake detection for a broad range of media, such as real-world images and videos. Furthermore, it proposes future research directions for tackling deepfake-related issues. Overall, this chapter aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the current state of deepfake technology.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement for a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being inherently conflicting. Thermochemical recycling of carbon and nitrogen in the massive atmosphere of a temperate exoplanet typically produces CH4 and NH3, while a small atmosphere atop a liquid water ocean would contain CO2 and N2, with the presence of photochemically produced CO and CH4, and reduced NH3 due to dissolution in the ocean. These distinctive atmospheric compositions produce distinctive features in the planet's transmission spectrum and emission phase curve, and multiple observations of a single planet could distinguish between models of its atmosphere and ocean chemistry, thereby informing assessments of its habitability potential. We apply this understanding to analyze the habitability potential of Kepler-10b, Kepler-38b, and V391 Persei b, with various assumptions about their atmospheric masses and solubilities of atmospheric gases in liquid water oceans. These studies highlight the need for precise measurements of the planet's radius, mass, and atmospheric properties, as well as the composition of its host star, to effectively assess the habitability of sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets. These data are essential for constraining models of the planet's interior and atmosphere, with the ultimate goal of understanding its habitability potential. Additionally, the analysis illustrates that observable differences between Earth-sized and massive atmospheres present unique opportunities to assess the habitability potential of temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets through multi-wavelength space missions and help inform planetary science studies during upcoming missions. The distinction between small vs. massive atmospheres may provide a new class of comparative planets that can be studied with existing and future space missions. The study shows that visible-light spectroscopy could potentially detect the atmospheric difference between Earth-sized and massive exoplanets over a specific range of irradiances, and that other planetary parameters could also influence this difference. Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns of binary vectors, an ability similar to that of symmetric Hopfield networks for spatial patterns. However,, MPN is capable of learning sequences up to a specific critical duration that is comparable to the memory capacity of binary Hopfield networks. The model's sequential learning capability is further exemplified by its ability to learn the natural language phonology of the FHO language, a formally defined language system. The computational efficiency of MPN has been found to be an order of magnitude better than that of comparable binary neural networks, a fact that is significant for its potential application in large-scale, hardware-efficient, spiking neural computers. Overall, the model provides a promising platform for exploring various aspects of computational neuroscience and the development of hardware neural computers. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of over 82,000 images, encompassing three text source types: synthetic, internet-based (remote), and handwritten.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a multi-source mixed dataset and a source-specific linear probing evaluation with two distinct data splits.
The research revealed a significant performance disparity between cutting-edge OCR models and a simple baseline in the unknown text instance setting.
The published paper includes a comprehensive analysis of the proposed models, while the code, dataset, and competition information are accessible via the link https://oov2022.github.io/. For any inquiries, please visit the GitHub repository at https://github.com/oov2022/oov2022.github.io.

The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and available resources. Moreover, industrial systems may exhibit multiple failure patterns, and individual sensor data often fails to unambiguously predict a specific malfunction. To address these issues, this research proposes an innovative solution centered on monitoring acyclic graphs representing complex relationships in high-dimensional data. By applying the concept of ancestral constraint to substructures within these graphs, we effectively reduce the focus to specific, individual sensors predicting a single failure. Our approach enables the exploration of ancestral relationships among high-dimensional data variables under certain conditions. We further develop a monitoring system to detect anomalies in such graphs, leveraging real-world examples from industrial environments to demonstrate the practical applicability of our solution. Our method exploits the topological structure present in high-dimensional data, as well as the conditional dependencies between variables, to facilitate efficient and scalable learning and operation of the method. We illustrate the performance of our solution through comparative studies involving artificial neural networks and the empirical analysis of industrial patterns in magnetometer and centrifuge data. We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that merged with the Milky Way's outer layers: the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 systems. Our sophisticated computational model, designed to simulate galaxy growth patterns, is based on exponential infall scenarios and allows for reliable fitting of these patterns. Our analysis led to the discovery of key time frames: 1.01 billion years for GSE to form new stars, while 10 billion years ago, the system experienced initial infall and then maintained its stellar formation for about 1.5-2 billion years. Conversely, the star-formation times for Wukong/LMS-1 were approximately 1.62 billion years. Our model showed strong consistency with predicted patterns in simulation-based research, with our findings indicating variations in growth patterns according to galaxy mass, a phenomenon also reflected in other research on galaxy development. Our unique computational method, coupled with data-driven research, has added depth to our comprehension of galaxy formation and development. Our analysis has provided new insights into the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that merged with the Milky Way, contributing to the broader understanding of galaxy growth and development patterns through our model's consistent prediction of these patterns. Given a profinite group G, an S[[G]]-module is a G-spectrum that fulfills certain criteria, leading to the definition of the homotopy orbit spectrum X_{hG} associated with an S[[G]]-module X. When X's constituents meet specific finiteness criteria, a homotopy orbit spectral sequence arises with an E2-term being the continuous homology of G, taking coefficients from the graded profinite \widehat{\mathbb{Z}}[[G]]-module \pi_*(X). This is demonstrated with an equivalence for certain conditions on G and Z: specifically, (Z[[G]])_{hG} is shown to be equivalent to Z in those scenarios, with supplementary methods for further investigation provided. Additionally, we establish that for connected profinite groups G, the homotopy orbit spectrum does not retain the connectedness property, using 2-Torus as a case study. Finally, we present a general statement regarding the homotopy orbit spectral sequence and its application to Z[[G]]-modules, revealing that the second sheet of the homotopy orbit spectral sequence exhibits bimodular decomposition properties for any profinite group G. This involves the formation of a bimodule over the Iwasawa algebra \Lambda(G), with a corresponding decomposition as a localized direct sum corresponding to a specific algebraic invariants equation. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is the limited availability of large, high-quality datasets suitable for deep learning. To address this issue, we developed a novel dataset of full-color, high-resolution invoices that can be effectively used for object classification, segmentation, and detection tasks. This custom dataset allows us to leverage the strengths of deep learning for complex document analysis by providing a sufficient number of examples, as well as detailed anatomical information about the structure of invoices. By doing so, we are able to replicate the level of detail found in real-world invoices without which models may struggle to generalize when applied to new, unseen documents. Furthermore, the visual representations in the dataset reveal the dynamic range found in scanned documents which can pose a challenge for deep learning-based approaches. We believe that this new dataset will play an important role in accelerating the advancement of automatic document analysis and will facilitate the advancement of state-of-the-art models for visually complex documents. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, Virgo, and the Advanced Very Large Array have observed a significant number of gravitational waves from compact binary mergers, which are mainly characterized by three types: binary black hole, binary neutron star, and heavy-stellar binary events. Their findings have facilitated numerous studies on the mass distribution of these events, but have been hindered by the difficulty in distinguishing binary neutron star events mixed with binary black hole events, particularly when the black hole mass is low. Therefore, in order to accurately analyze the full spectrum of gravitational wave events detected by LIGO-Virgo, it is essential to improve the ability to distinguish binary neutron star and low-mass binary black hole events. In this context, we have developed a method called Wavefunction Inversion, which utilizes the analytic waveforms of the two systems to calculate their cross-correlation and assign probabilities to each other based on the measured strain data. By applying this method to two days of Virgo's run called O3G, we were able to successfully classify 16 out of 18 candidate binary neutron star events that were previously undifferentiated from binary black hole events. In a realistic scenario of actual detection, we found that Wavefunction Inversion would have correctly identified 60% of the mixed events, and would have avoided false positives in 90% of the remaining cases. We believe that Wavefunction Inversion will be a valuable tool to enhance the ability of future gravitational wave observatories to distinguish binary neutron star and low-mass binary black hole events. In addition, this method can be utilized for the joint analysis of gravitational wave and electromagnetic observations of these events. In the near future, we anticipate that the ability of Wavefunction Inversion to classify gravitational wave events will be improved through the incorporation of higher-order post-Newtonian predictions for the cross-correlation of the two types of binary mergers. Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by an extremely vast number of states and actions, as well as a difficult-to-compute transition matrix. To resolve these challenges, we develop an algorithm that combines policy iteration with subgradient ascent. We show that this approach allows the CMDP to converge to a solution at a rate proportional to $O(\log(T)/\sqrt{T})$, where T represents the number of iterations, provided that a specific condition is met. This method also offers an efficient way to reduce the dimensionality of the CMDP by exploiting its structural properties when applicable. We successfully apply our algorithm to critical problems with such a structure: multi-product inventory control and multi-class queue management, achieving results superior to state-of-art methods. Moreover, we demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm through numerical experiments on these problems. Where possible, we also utilize an recently developed technique for dimensionality reduction - hyperplane method - in order to decrease the number of actions and dimensions of the CMDP. For instance, in multi-product inventory we have reduced the number of actions from O(N^2) to O(N), where N is the number of products. This allows us to solve a CMDP with 100 products in approximately 1 second, whereas an un-reduced version would take approximately 6 hours. Similarly, in multi-class queue we have reduced the number of actions from O(N^2 M) to O(N + M), where N is the number of customers and M is the number of classes. This allows us to solve a CMDP in a scenario with 100 customers and 6 classes in approximately 0.2 seconds, whereas an un-reduced version would take approximately 900 seconds. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields secure and stable navigation in unstructured indoor environments. Moreover, the method's modularity allows for the exploration of various sensor configurations, thus facilitating the study of its robustness and adaptability across diverse navigation tasks. For example, maintaining wheel elevation above ground level ensures that the system can still function during light rain, through raising the potential for future incorporation of radar and ladar sensors. This research has potential applications in mobile robot navigation in security and defense settings, as well as autonomous driving within inclement weather conditions. Upon determining the divisibility of N, we outline a step-by-step method to precisely calculate the pair of symmetrical quotients, if such a pair exists. This method involves an algorithm that decomposes N into its prime factors and subsequent processing of these factors to construct the desired symmetrical quotient pairs. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  This performance advantage is attributed to DynaSOAr's ability to efficiently manage memory and achieve a general 2 to 6 times performance improvement over corresponding host code speedup.  In addition to memory benefits, DynaSOAr's speedup of up to 60 times over corresponding host code can also be attributed to its ability to effectively utilize a large number of threads.  Validation of our previous theoretical findings on the challenge of allocating memory in parallel, while managing access to the heap, is also provided through our experimental results.  As a contribution to the field, the DynaSOAr framework and associated performance improvements are now freely accessible to the public under an OSI-approved license.  Specifically, the framework is made available under the terms of the permissive BSD license to ensure ease of adoption by other researchers.  An online documentation of the framework is also maintained for ease of use by other researchers.  As a result of this contribution, the DynaSOAr framework has become a valuable resource for other researchers in the field.  Further details about the project can be found online at https://github.com/alexeyev/dyna-soar.  An overview of the project's code structure and organization is provided

To incorporate quantum gravity effects, we propose the introduction of a Dirac fermion χ as a dark matter candidate that's odd under gauged Z2 symmetry post U(1)X breaking, leading to a natural realization of isospin-violating dark matter with a natural f_n/f_p ratio of -0.7, thereby evading LUX, PANDAX and XENON1T experimental constraints. To determine LHC Z' mass bounds for generic U(1)X models, four different scenarios are examined, with scenario II featuring no U(1)X charge for right-handed up-type quarks allowing a relaxation in the LHC Z' mass bound. Moreover, our work introduces LHC relevance beyond key model parameters through gauge coupling unity and dark matter mass requirements. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital logic section. With a single resistive network connecting the PMOS circuit and two parallel oscillators, the design exhibits improved thermal monitoring capabilities while minimizing power consumption, achieving a temperature standard deviation of 0.45% and a frequency standard deviation of 2.78% over the temperature range of 0 to 100 degrees Celsius. The proposed temperature sensor has a compact footprint of 0.38 mm x 0.38 mm on a 180 nm CMOS process and operates within frequency ranges of 200 kHz to 6 MHz. The computational efficiency of the sensor module allows it to generate a digital temperature code within 5.84 microseconds. The temperature sensor has the capability to run on a custom frequency, generated either from an external clock or an on-chip free-running oscillator. The design also incorporates two clock generation blocks that can produce frequencies proportional to temperature for the sensor module's operation, achieving a minimum frequency of 200 kHz and a maximum frequency of 6 MHz. The measurement results confirm the performance efficiency of the designed temperature sensor. The research showcases a next-generation temperature sensing solution, offering high accuracy, low power consumption, and advanced features such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling compatibility and a frequency-based temperature measurement output. The proposed temperature sensor architecture is highly suitable for modern SoC designs. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired hybrid entangled states, which are a combination of both discrete and continuous variables. We present two methods of implementing this technique using a non-dump mode approach, one method utilizing a single spontaneous parametric down conversion source and the other a combination of a beam splitter and two parametric down conversion sources. By applying the quantum scissors technique, it is possible to create entangled photon spin and polarization entanglement, thereby opening up the possibility of utilizing a variety of resources that have been previously overlooked. We demonstrate theoretically that the created entangled states can be used in executing multiple quantum information tasks including teleportation of any polarization state, generating entangled multi-photon states, and maximizing the success probability in a Bell test, outperforming current technologies that utilize postselection or destructive detection. This research represents a significant advancement in the field of entangled photon generation and associated quantum information technologies. Based on these alternative definitions, the authors establish lower bounds for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm in these scenarios. Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes; yet current approaches disregard the costs involved in extracting device features from network data. This work presents a more practical viewpoint, contending that feature extraction comes with expenses varying across distinct features. Moving beyond existing binary misclassification assessments, this research suggests adopting multiple loss measures according to device feature extraction costs, thus introducing the first probabilistic learning framework for IoT device classification after feature extraction. The approach utilizes Bayesian Networks to address this task and is evaluated using a widely-used dataset, with results showing that considering feature extraction costs leads to heightened loss and decreased accuracy compared to the basic method. Nevertheless, this model can function as a standalone device classification system or be integrated with other approaches, with potential to improve accuracy through feature extraction optimization. Moreover, this model can facilitate feature extraction optimization by quantifying every feature's value in minimizing loss. This framework offers a novel viewpoint on IoT device classification and can serve as a starting point for exploring cost-related issues in machine learning. Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators. Additionally, the study introduces a binary relation on the free algebra over the free forest generated by a set of variables, generalizing the concept of forcing in classical logic. The study demonstrates that this relation corresponds to the truth table meaning of a particular Godel modal logic formula with variables. Furthermore, the study shows the existence of a Kripke-style semantics for Godel modal logics based on finite forests with single accessibility, through a modification of standard intutionistic modal logic semantics rules. The study also provides a Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorem for this type of semantics. Ultimately, the study showcases the symmetry between algebraic and relational properties of finite Godel modal algebras and the corresponding relationship between their dual structures and the studied forest frames. The study proposes utilizing relational structures as a prelinear alternative to traditional classical and intutionistic modal logic semantics, thanks to their simplicity and clarity in specific logical systems. The study encourages further research into other advanced modal logics within the same framework. The study also offers a fresh perspective on existing intutionistic modal logic results. The existence of both single and double accessibility relation structures in Godel modal logics provides a common ground for the comparison of positive and classical logics with intutionistic modal logics. The study reveals the possibility of interpreting classical logic operators as prelinear modal operators on the free algebra over the free forest generated by a set of variables with a binary relation, through the utilization of the existing relation. We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, under the condition that only repulsive interactions were present. We discovered that systems with $\eta < 0.5$ exhibit isotropic and nematic liquid crystalline phases, whereas the system with $\eta = 0.5$ is in a metastable state and the system with $\eta > 0.5$ exhibits unconventional polar smectic and paramagnetic phases, alongside the nematic and isotropic ones. The introduced model shows similar behavior to that of earlier proposed models for polar fluids and displays unique characteristics of wedge-shaped molecules. The system's energy as a function of polar angle of the first nematic liquid crystal layer showed that it is minimized at an angle that decreases as the parameter $d$ increases, up to a point where the system transitions into a polar smectic phase. We introduce a simple model that explains how the uniform ferroelectric polarization of the nematic and isotropic phases is developed. Additionally, we discovered that system responses correlate the dimension of the system with the dimension of the system containing only non-interacting hard rackets, based on the principle of dimensional reasoning. Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom. Additionally, we also find that any sharp feature within an inflationary model can introduce classical oscillations, where the signs can potentially be informed through upcoming CMB-S4 observations, and different scenarios can be distinguished from one another. Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the exploration of latent spaces, providing insights into the complex concepts, like 'carbon emission,' learned by the model. We illustrate the Stable Artist's capabilities through multiple tasks, demonstrating its ability to create high-quality, tailored images and compositions. The associated code can be found on the Stable Artist GitHub repository. Visual demonstrations are available on YouTube. Additionally, the generated images can be accessed on our website. All created images are original and produced using our method.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of model uncertainty into Bayesian deep learning. We propose a novel approach called 'Ensemble approximate inference' that simultaneously measures epistemic and idiosyncratic uncertainty, thereby enhancing the accuracy of predictive models. Furthermore, we develop a new method called 'Uncertainty-based Steganography' that effectively utilizes the predictive distribution and uncertainty measures to achieve higher quality of steganographic images while increasing the capacity of steganographic messages. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods in reversible steganography. The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the video transformer network. Building on existing research into vision transformer architectures, we address the limitations associated with their high computational complexity and data-hungry nature. To achieve this, we propose combining Video Swin-Transformer with a dedicated data augmentation method, and employing a gradual learning approach with adaptive learning rates. The efficacy of our proposed approach was tested on the Weather4Cast III challenge dataset, where we successfully predicted 8 hours of future weather frames from hourly weather sequences. The experimental results demonstrate the significant contribution of each component to the overall performance, with the complete model achieving an accuracy of 64.2% on the validation set, and 63.9% on the test set. This achievement places our approach among the top performing models in the challenge leaderboard. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/deweyofsparta/WeatherForecast.git.

Specifically, we analyze the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models that allow softly broken $S_3$ terms, determining which models can host dark matter. The variety of models arises from different arrangements of vacuum expectation values, leading to vacua with either one or two vanishing expectation values. In our research, we consider a scenario where the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, a remnant of $S_3$, stabilizes the dark matter candidate. Our study focuses on two models: one with CP violation and another without, each consisting of a single dark matter candidate and two active scalar sectors behaving similarly to a Type-I two-Higgs-doublet model. After investigating these models under various constraints, we identified potential masses for the dark matter candidate. In the case with CP violation, we found possible mass ranges of $[52.5, 89]~\text{GeV}$ or $[6.5, 44.5]~\text{GeV}$. For the model without CP violation, we found possible mass ranges of $[55.5, 89]~\text{GeV}$ or $[6.5, 44.5]~\text{GeV}$. Additionally, we calculated the exact unitarity matrix and predicted Higgs boson production and decay modes relevant to future collider searches for these scalar particles. Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural structures, enabling their survival and operation. Disruption of this process is associated with various neurodegenerative diseases, making it vital to understand how neurons control transportation to target essential areas. We introduce a new optimization model that simulates the material transportation mechanism in complex neural geometries by minimizing congestion. The model adheres to partial differential equations that describe transportation based on molecular-motor-assisted models and is solved within complex tree structures through isogeometric analysis. We test our model by examining the optimal transport rate of a material, such as vesicles, through optimizations problems with and without constraints on the material's flow rate. The simulations demonstrate that optimizing this process can uncover important insights into how neurons control transportation to different parts of the cell.
